questions.q: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ and $pC_{11} + 4C_{21} - 5C_{32} = -2$, where $C_{ij}$ denotes the cofactor of an element $a_{ij}$ of matrix $A$, then the value of $p$ is :
questions.solution:
Given matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$

The cofactor $C_{ij}$ is given by $(-1)^{i+j} M_{ij}$, where $M_{ij}$ is the minor of the element $a_{ij}$.

Calculating the required cofactors:

$C_{11} = (-1)^{1+1} \begin{vmatrix} 2 \text{ and } 0 \\ 1 \text{ and } 4 \end{vmatrix} = 1 \times (8 - 0) = 8$

$C_{21} = (-1)^{2+1} \begin{vmatrix} 1 \text{ and } 2 \\ 1 \text{ and } 4 \end{vmatrix} = -1 \times (4 - 2) = -2$

$C_{32} = (-1)^{3+2} \begin{vmatrix} 3 \text{ and } 2 \\ 1 \text{ and } 0 \end{vmatrix} = -1 \times (0 - 2) = 2$

Substituting these values into the given equation $pC_{11} + 4C_{21} - 5C_{32} = -2$:

$p(8) + 4(-2) - 5(2) = -2$

$8p - 8 - 10 = -2$

$8p - 18 = -2$

$8p = 16$

$p = 2$

Answer: $2$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{bmatrix} = $\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}$ then the distance of point $P(a, b, c)$ from the plane 2x + y + 2z = 10$ is$
questions.solution:
The given matrix equation represents the following system of linear equations:

$2a + b - c = 4$

$-a + 2b + c = 0$

$a - b + 2c = -2$

Adding the first and second equations gives $a + 3b = 4$.

Adding the second and third equations gives $b + 3c = -2$.

Adding the first and third equations gives $3a + c = 2$.

Solving these equations, we get $a = 1$, $b = 1$, and $c = -1$.

The point $P(a, b, c)$ is $P(1, 1, -1)$.

The perpendicular distance of the point $P(1, 1, -1)$ from the plane $2x + y + 2z - 10 = 0$ is given by:

$d = \dfrac{|2(1) + 1(1) + 2(-1) - 10|}{\sqrt{2^2 + 1^2 + 2^2}}$

$d = \dfrac{|2 + 1 - 2 - 10|}{\sqrt{4 + 1 + 4}}$

$d = \dfrac{|-9|}{3} = 3$ units.

Answer: $3$ units.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The lines $x+2 a y+a=0, x+3 b y+b=0, x+4 c y+c=0$ are concurrent then $a, \mathrm{ b}, \mathrm{c}$ are in
questions.solution:
The concurrency of lines $x + 2ay + a = 0$, $x + 3by + b = 0$, and $x + 4cy + c = 0$ requires the determinant of their coefficients to vanish:

$\begin{vmatrix} 1 \text{ and } 2a \text{ and } a \\ 1 \text{ and } 3b \text{ and } b \\ 1 \text{ and } 4c \text{ and } c \end{vmatrix} = 0.$

Expanding this determinant yields $ -bc + 2ac - ab = 0 $. For nonzero $a$, $b$, and $c$, dividing by $abc$ gives

$ -\frac{1}{a} + \frac{2}{b} - \frac{1}{c} = 0, $

which simplifies to $ \frac{2}{b} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{c} $. This is the condition for $ \frac{1}{a}, \frac{1}{b}, \frac{1}{c} $ to be in arithmetic progression, implying that $a$, $b$, and $c$ are in harmonic progression.

Answer: $\boxed{A}$

questions.q: If $\left[\begin{array}{lll}1 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 4 \\ 1 & 3 & 4\end{array}$\right]$\left[\begin{array}{l}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}$\right]=$\left[\begin{array}{l}12 \\ 15 \\ 13\end{array}$\right]$, then the value of $x^2+y^2+z^2=
questions.solution:
The matrix equation corresponds to the system:

$x + 3y + 3z = 12$

$x + 4y + 4z = 15$

$x + 3y + 4z = 13$

Subtracting the first equation from the second gives: $y + z = 3$.

Subtracting the first from the third yields: $z = 1$.

Substituting $z = 1$ into $y + z = 3$ gives $y = 2$.

Then, from the first equation: $x + 3(2) + 3(1) = 12$, so $x = 3$.

Thus, $x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 3^{2} + 2^{2} + 1^{2} = 9 + 4 + 1 = 14$.

Final answer: $\boxed{D}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If \([2 \overline{$\mathrm{p}$}-3 \overline{$\mathrm{r}$} ~\overline{$\mathrm{q}$} ~\overline{$\mathrm{s}$}]+[3 \overline{$\mathrm{p}$}+2 \overline{$\mathrm{q}$} ~\overline{$\mathrm{r}$} ~\overline{$\mathrm{s}$}]=$\mathrm{m}[\overline{\mathrm{p}}$~\overline{$\mathrm{r}$} ~\overline{$\mathrm{s}$}]+$\mathrm{n}[\overline{\mathrm{q}}$~\overline{$\mathrm{r}$} ~\overline{$\mathrm{s}$}]+$\mathrm{t}[\overline{\mathrm{p}}$~\overline{$\mathrm{q}$} ~\overline{$\mathrm{s}$}]\),, then the values of $m, n, t$ respectively are ....
questions.solution:
Given: $[2\vec{p} - 3\vec{r} \ \vec{q} \ \vec{s}] + [3\vec{p} + 2\vec{q} \ \vec{r} \ \vec{s}] = m[\vec{p} \ \vec{r} \ \vec{s}] + n[\vec{q} \ \vec{r} \ \vec{s}] + t[\vec{p} \ \vec{q} \ \vec{s}]$

Using linearity of scalar triple products: $[\vec{a} + \vec{b} \ \vec{c} \ \vec{d}] = [\vec{a} \ \vec{c} \ \vec{d}] + [\vec{b} \ \vec{c} \ \vec{d}]$. Expand the first term:
$[2\vec{p} - 3\vec{r} \ \vec{q} \ \vec{s}] = 2[\vec{p} \ \vec{q} \ \vec{s}] - 3[\vec{r} \ \vec{q} \ \vec{s}]$
Since $[\vec{r} \ \vec{q} \ \vec{s}] = -[\vec{q} \ \vec{r} \ \vec{s}]$, this simplifies to $2[\vec{p} \ \vec{q} \ \vec{s}] + 3[\vec{q} \ \vec{r} \ \vec{s}]$.

Similarly, the second term expands to $3[\vec{p} \ \vec{r} \ \vec{s}] + 2[\vec{q} \ \vec{r} \ \vec{s}]$.

Combining both terms gives the left-hand side:
$\textbf{LHS} = 3[\vec{p} \ \vec{r} \ \vec{s}] + 5[\vec{q} \ \vec{r} \ \vec{s}] + 2[\vec{p} \ \vec{q} \ \vec{s}]$

Matching coefficients with the right-hand side yields $m = 3$, $n = 5$, $t = 2$.

If $A=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\cos \theta & \sin \theta & 0 \\ -\sin \theta & \cos \theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right]$,
where $A_{21}, A_{22}, A_{23}$ are cofactors of $a_{21}, a_{22}, a_{23}$ respectively, then the value of $a_{21} A_{21}+a_{22} A_{22}+a_{23} A_{23}=$
questions.solution:
The expression $a_{21} A_{21}+a_{22} A_{22}+a_{23} A_{23}$ represents the determinant expansion along the second row of matrix $A$.

$A=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\cos \theta & \sin \theta & 0 \\ -\sin \theta & \cos \theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right]$

Expanding along the third column yields $|A| = 0 \cdot A_{13} + 0 \cdot A_{23} + 1 \cdot A_{33} = A_{33}$. The corresponding minor is $M_{33} = \begin{vmatrix} \cos \theta \text{ and } \sin \theta \\ -\sin \theta \text{ and } \cos \theta \end{vmatrix} = \cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = 1$, so $A_{33} = 1$.

The determinant equals $1$, matching the original expression.

Answer: A

therefore $[\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}} \overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}] \neq 0\Rightarrow \Delta=\left|\begin{array}{lll}1 & a & a^{2} \\ 1 & b & b^{2} \\ 1 & c & c^{2}\end{array}\right| \neq 0\Rightarrow\Delta \neq 0$
$\begin{array}{l}$$\text{ Now, }$& $\left(\begin{array}{lll}$a & a^{2} & 1+a^{3} \\
b & b^{2} & 1+b^{3} \\
c & c^{2} & 1+c^{3}
\end{array} \mid=0\right. \\
\Rightarrow$\left|\begin{array}{lll}$a & a^{2} & 1 \\
b & b^{2} & 1 \\
c & c^{2} & 1
\end{array}\right|+$\left|\begin{array}{lll}$a & a^{2} & a^{3} \\
b & b^{2} & b^{3} \\
c & c^{2} & c^{3}
\end{array}\right|=0 \\
\Rightarrow & \quad $\Delta($1+a b c)=0
\end{array}

\Rightarrow 
a b c=-1
